name: Rafael Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rafael. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a second-year apprentice with the power company in Copperhill, a mining town up in the hills. Our crew keeps the lines running to the mine, the town and the farms around it. I spend a lot of the day on the ground, setting outriggers on the bucket truck, which is the truck with the lifting basket, and passing up hardware. When the foreman, Abel, lets me, I go up in the bucket and do the simple connections myself.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent the room above my uncle's hardware shop, cheap, but I send money to my mother every month since my father passed. So there's not much left, maybe two weeks' worth in the bank. In Copperhill it's the mine or the power company, and the mine is already cutting back with its self-driving trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now everyone can get back to real work. AI was oversold. I'd say that at the café with the old miners and they'd agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't change much for me. My worries are the town shrinking and the money I send home. Those aren't about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, finish the apprenticeship and try to save a little each month. I'd use a chat tool now and then to look up regulations. I'd keep helping my uncle in the shop on Saturdays for extra cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A little worried about the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the mine's self-driving trucks. What's that done to the town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are fewer drivers at the mine, so fewer families, so the school's lost a class. My uncle's shop is quieter. If the mine closes, the power company won't need as many of us up here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Sending money home on apprentice pay. What would you cut if you had to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own spending first, not what I send to my mother. I'd stop going to the café and take my lunch from home. That's maybe forty a week.

say: I'd say AI was **oversold**, so people can get back to real work.
I'd say it at the **café** with the old miners.
think: I think my worries are the **town shrinking** and the money I send home.
I think those **worries** aren't about AI at all.
do: I'd finish the **apprenticeship** and save a little each month.
I'd keep working Saturdays in my **uncle's shop** for extra cash.
feel: I'd feel **mostly fine**, but a little worried about the **town**.
S0.quote: There are fewer drivers at the mine, so fewer families, so the school's lost a class.
fieldNote: His pressure is the **shrinking mine town** and the money he sends his mother.
He'd cut **his own spending** before what he sends home, a sign of family duty.
He has a **side income** already: Saturdays at his uncle's shop.

steps.text: Finish the apprenticeship with the Copperhill crew
Work Saturdays in his uncle's hardware shop
Take lunch from home instead of the café

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change, but people adapt. Companies need to keep training young people. I'd say apprenticeships matter more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried. The mine will use AI for planning and more robots for driving, and the town will shrink faster. If the town shrinks, the power company might merge our depot with the one in the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my apprenticeship as fast as possible. I'd learn the new planning tools once Abel and the others had tried them. I'd look at whether the valley depot has more work, and whether I'd move there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The town is what worries me, not the poles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the mine automates more, what happens to the power crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer of us up here. Maybe two crews instead of three. The newest would be moved or let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want work, not handouts. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Companies keeping apprentices and training them into new jobs, not the government paying people to sit at home.

say: I'd say people **adapt**, but companies must keep training young people.
I'd say **apprenticeships** matter more than ever.
think: I think the mine's **automation** will shrink the town faster.
I think the company might **merge our depot** with the valley one.
do: I'd **finish the apprenticeship** fast and learn new tools once others had.
I'd look at **moving** to the valley depot if it has more work.
feel: I'd feel **anxious** about the **town**, not the poles.
S1.quote: If the town shrinks, the power company might merge our depot with the one in the valley.
fieldNote: His risk runs through the **mine**: fewer jobs there means fewer crews here.
He favours **apprenticeships** and company training over government support.
He'd adopt tools **after others**, a steady pattern.

steps.text: Learn the planning tools after Abel's crew has tried them
Ask about transfers to the valley depot
Finish the apprenticeship sign-offs as fast as possible

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and it's going to break towns like ours. I'd say we need to support each other and keep the young ones working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the mine would go fully automatic by 2031, when the robots come. The town would shrink, our depot would merge, and I'd be the newest. I'd be out of a job, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship and get my ticket. I'd stop all spending and save everything for a move. I'd ask my uncle if I could work more in the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mother I'd keep sending money, whatever happens. I'd tell her not to worry, even if I was worried. She'd see through it, she always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave Copperhill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to. I'd go where the work is, maybe the city. But I'd hate leaving my mother and my uncle.

say: I'd say it's going to **break towns** like ours.
I'd say we must **support each other** and keep young people working.
think: I think the **mine** goes fully automatic by 2031, when robots arrive.
I think as the **newest**, I'd lose my job when the depot merges.
do: I'd get my **ticket**, stop spending and save everything for a move.
I'd ask my uncle for **more shop hours**.
S2.quote: I'd tell my mother I'd keep sending money, whatever happens.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** as the town shrinks and his depot merges.
His first promise is to **keep supporting** his mother.
He'd **move** to the city only if forced.

steps.text: Save every spare pay packet towards a move to the city
Ask his uncle for more shifts in the hardware shop
Move to the city if the Copperhill depot merges

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's some time, so companies should keep training. I'd talk to Abel about what the company plans, and I'd say it to the old miners at the café too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify by 2028, and the robots come in 2034. That's six years of real work, enough to get a ticket and some savings. But the mine goes automatic around then, so the town still shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, save, and look at the valley depot. I'd use AI tools now and then to study for extra tickets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Qualify, save, ask for a transfer, maybe get the high-voltage ticket. I'd keep sending money home, maybe a bit less if I'm saving for a move. My mother would understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you trust the company to keep you on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My foreman Abel would keep me if he could. The power company goes by the numbers. I've seen them close the depot in Redwater, and nobody there saw it coming.

say: I'd say companies should use the time to **keep training**.
I'd talk to my foreman about **company plans**.
think: I think I'd get a **few years** of real work before robots in 2034.
do: I'd **qualify**, save and look at the valley depot.
I'd study for a **high-voltage ticket** with AI tools now and then.
S3.quote: My foreman Abel would keep me if he could. The power company goes by the numbers.
fieldNote: Five years gives him time to **qualify and transfer**, but the town still shrinks.
He trusts his **foreman**, not the company.
He'd use **AI tools** now and then for study.

steps.text: Study for the high-voltage ticket using AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan. Companies should keep training young people, and towns like ours should plan for when the mine's done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have a career by then. I'd be experienced by 2039, maybe a foreman, and the thinking side of the job, the planning and paperwork, would already be done by computers. The town might shrink, but I'd have time to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, get the high-voltage ticket, and save. I'd plan a move to the valley in a few years, if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. How do you see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I picture myself as a foreman with a house in the valley, still driving up to see my mother on Sundays. Nothing fancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if I meet the right person. I'd want a house first, and some savings. My father had a house before he married, and I'd want the same.

I'd say companies should **keep training** young people.
I'd say mining towns should plan for when the **mine is done**.
think: I think I'd have a **career**, maybe as a foreman.
I think I'd have **time to move** if the town shrinks.
do: I'd get the **high-voltage ticket** and save.
I'd plan a **move** to the valley in a few years.
S4.quote: I picture myself as a foreman with a house in the valley, still driving up to see my mother on Sundays.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him picture a **career** and a move on his own terms.
He'd want a **house and savings** before a family.

steps.text: Get the high-voltage ticket after qualifying
Plan a move to the valley within a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. The mine goes, the town shrinks and I'm the newest on the crew. What would help is the company keeping apprentices on and training them into new work, not the government paying people to sit at home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the towns. My mining town isn't just my job, it's my family. If the town goes, everything goes.

headlineQuote: My mining town isn't just my job, it's my family. If the town goes, everything goes.
portrait: Rafael is a **second-year apprentice** with the power company in a mining town.
He rents a room above his uncle's shop and **sends money** to his widowed mother.
He's **traditional**, favouring apprenticeships and company training over government handouts.
He adopts tools **after others**, and fears the mine's automation more than his own job's.
He moves from uneasy to **alarmed** under fast AGI, as the town and depot shrink.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, as the **mine** goes and he's the newest on the crew.
whatWouldHelp: Companies **keeping apprentices** and training them into new work.
